course.title: SQL schema design and constraints
course.description: Primary and foreign keys, NOT NULL, UNIQUE and CHECK as the last line of defence, what normalisation protects, and keeping a unique rule alive next to soft delete.

lessons.title: SQL schema design and constraints
lessons.explanation: Primary and foreign keys, NOT NULL, UNIQUE and CHECK as the last line of defence, what normalisation protects, and keeping a unique rule alive next to soft delete.

unit.title: Write DDL that rejects bad rows

tests.name: valid users and orders are accepted
a duplicate email is rejected
a user without an email is rejected, even twice (trap)
an order for a user that does not exist is rejected
a quantity of zero or less is rejected, a quantity of 1 is fine (boundary)
an order without a user or without a quantity is rejected
a user who still has orders cannot be deleted

unit.title: Unique email among users that are not soft-deleted

tests.name: live users with different emails are accepted
a second live user with the same email is rejected
a soft-deleted user does not block signing up again
several soft-deleted rows may share an email and a deletion time (boundary)
restoring a deleted user whose email is live again is rejected (trap)

unit.title: At most one primary address per customer

tests.name: a customer can have several non-primary addresses
one primary address next to other addresses is accepted
a second primary address for the same customer is rejected
two customers each keep their own primary address
is_primary accepts no value other than 0 and 1 (trap)
the primary flag can move when the old one is cleared first (boundary)

fund-js/30-sql-schema-design-and-constra.instructions:
**Skills:** NOT NULL · UNIQUE · FOREIGN KEY · CHECK  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "Here are two tables with no constraints. Which bad rows can get in, and how do you stop them?"

**Why it matters.** Validation in application code runs in one code path and races with itself. A constraint runs for every writer: the API, the admin script, the migration, the colleague with a SQL console.

**Your task.** Export `ddl`, a SQL string that creates two tables. The tests run it on a real in-memory SQLite database with foreign-key enforcement switched on, then try to insert bad rows. Keep these table and column names:
- `users(id, email)` with `id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`
- `orders(id, user_id, qty)` with `id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY`

The database must reject:
- a second user with an email that is already present
- a user without an email
- an order whose `user_id` matches no user, and an order without a `user_id`
- an order whose `qty` is missing, zero or negative
- deleting a user who still has orders

**Worked example.** After `ddl` has run, inserting the email `ada@example.com` twice makes the second insert throw a constraint error, and the table still holds one row.
hints: Each rule in the list maps to one kind of column constraint, and most constraints say nothing about a missing value.
Go through the rejected rows one by one and name the constraint that stops each. Then ask of every constrained column what happens when the value is absent.

Make the email required and unique, make the order point at an existing user with a required reference, and require a quantity that a check keeps above zero. Leave the delete behaviour at its default.

fund-js/30-sql-schema-design-and-constra.instructions:
**Skills:** partial index · soft delete · UNIQUE and NULL  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "We soft-delete users. Now nobody can sign up again with the email of a deleted account. Fix it without losing the unique rule."

**Why it matters.** Soft delete changes what "unique" means: unique among the rows that are still alive. A plain unique constraint is too strict, and the obvious two-column constraint is not a constraint at all.

**The table.** The tests create `users(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT NOT NULL, deleted_at TEXT)`. A live user has a NULL `deleted_at`; deleting a user sets it to a timestamp.

**Your task.** Export `index`, a SQL string holding one `CREATE UNIQUE INDEX` statement on `users`. The tests run it and then insert and update rows. After it:
- two live users can never have the same email
- a soft-deleted user does not block a new user with the same email
- any number of soft-deleted rows may share an email, even with the same `deleted_at`
- restoring a deleted user (setting `deleted_at` back to NULL) is rejected when a live user already has that email

**Worked example.** Ada signs up, is soft-deleted, and signs up again: two rows with her email, one deleted and one live. A third sign-up with that email is rejected.
fund-js/30-sql-schema-design-and-constra.explanation:
```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_live ON users (email) WHERE deleted_at IS NULL
```

A partial index contains only the rows that satisfy its `WHERE`. Deleted rows are simply not in it, so they can repeat an email freely; live rows are all in it, so they cannot. An update that brings a row back into the index (a restore) is checked like an insert, which is why the trap test's restore fails.

The plausible wrong answer is `UNIQUE (email, deleted_at)`. It looks like "unique per deletion state", but every live row has a NULL in the second column and NULLs are distinct, so two live rows with one email are accepted: the test "a second live user with the same email is rejected" catches it. It also rejects two rows deleted at the same instant. A plain unique index on `email` fails the other way and blocks the new sign-up.

The statement is valid in Postgres as written. MySQL has no partial indexes; there the usual workaround is a generated column that is NULL for deleted rows.
hints: An index does not have to contain every row of its table.
Describe in words which rows the unique rule applies to, and build the index over that subset only, leaving the others out.
Create a unique index on the email column and end the statement with a filter that keeps only rows whose deletion timestamp is NULL.

fund-js/30-sql-schema-design-and-constra.instructions:
**Skills:** partial unique index · CHECK · schema repair  
**Level:** ★★★

**Interview prompt.** "Some customers have two primary addresses and the shipping label printer picks one at random. The code sets the flag correctly. How did this happen, and how do you make it impossible?"

**Why it matters.** "Unset the old one, set the new one" in application code is two statements. Two requests interleave, or one fails halfway, and the data breaks a rule that no line of the schema states.

**The table.** The tests create `customers(id, name)` and then run your DDL. The starter holds the production schema of `addresses`: `is_primary` is a plain integer flag.

**Your task.** Export `ddl`, a SQL string that creates `addresses(id, customer_id, line, is_primary)` (keep those names; `is_primary` stays an integer that defaults to 0) plus whatever else is needed so that:
- a customer can have any number of addresses with `is_primary` 0
- a customer can have at most one address with `is_primary` 1
- different customers each have their own primary address
- `is_primary` accepts no value other than 0 and 1
- moving the primary flag works when the old address is cleared first; setting a second one without clearing is rejected

**Worked example.** Ada has a primary address "1 Main St" and a second address "9 Side Rd". Inserting "9 Side Rd" with `is_primary` 1 is rejected; inserting it with 0 is accepted.
fund-js/30-sql-schema-design-and-constra.explanation:
```sql
CREATE TABLE addresses (
  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id INTEGER NOT NULL REFERENCES customers (id),
  line TEXT NOT NULL,
  is_primary INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0 CHECK (is_primary IN (0, 1))
);
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX addresses_one_primary ON addresses (customer_id) WHERE is_primary = 1;
```

The partial index holds only the primary rows, and inside it `customer_id` must be unique: one primary per customer, no limit on the rest.

The plausible wrong answer is the table constraint `UNIQUE (customer_id, is_primary)`. It does stop a second primary, but it equally stops a second NON-primary address, because the pair (1, 0) may also appear only once. The first test catches it.

The `CHECK` matters too. Without it a row with `is_primary = 2` is outside the index, yet application code that tests the flag for truthiness treats it as primary: the rule is broken again through a side door. The trap test catches a schema that leaves it out.

Moving the flag takes two updates in one transaction, old row first. In Postgres the column would be a boolean and the index would end in `WHERE is_primary`. Another sound design drops the flag and stores `primary_address_id` on the customer row.
hints: A unique rule can apply to a subset of the rows in a table.
State the rule as: among the rows flagged as primary, each customer appears once. Then make sure the flag itself cannot hold a value outside the two you expect.
Add a check that limits the flag to zero or one, and create a unique index on the customer id that is filtered to rows where the flag equals one.
